div.head: Leis Wl 29.1
div.ab: ne leist a seignurage departir les cultivurs de lur terre, pur tant cum il pussent le dreit seirvise faire.
nec licet dominis remouere colonos a terris, dummodo debita seruitia persoluant.
ne leist a seignurage departir les cultivurs de lur terre, pur tant cum il pussent le dreit seirvise faire.
29, 1 noch auch ist es der Herrschaft erlaubt, die Bauern von deren Lande zu entfernen, sofern sie den richtigen Dienst leisten können.
29, 1 nor is it permitted to the lordship to remove the peasants from their land, so long as they can perform the proper service.
It is not permitted to estate-owners to eject the cultivators from their land, as long as they can perform their legal service.

note.seg: from their holding to the lord of the manor

Ebd. Bauer 10b; Fron. Nach Dial. de scacc. I 10 C. 11 B.C durften zwar anfangs nach 1066 die Angelsachsen [auf Dorfboden, in Bauerstellen] pro voluntate dominorum a possessionibus pell[i], erhielten dann aber sicheren Besitz, und nur die Domänen-ascriptitii a dominis suis ad alia loca transferri possunt, venduntur vel distrahuntur. Jene staatliche Aufsicht über die Beziehung zwischen Herrschaftsgut und Villan, gerichtet gegen die im 12. Jh. bisweilen nachweisbare Austreibung oder Verpflanzung von Villanen, ist älter als die Epoche Heinrichs II., in der die Zuständigkeit über Villane der Kronjustiz verloren ging; Vinogradoff Villain. 159. 165. 219; Maitland Domesday 62.—Vielleicht lag dieser Satz in L Bracton vor: einstige Freibauern auf ‘Alter Krondomäne’ [nur davon spricht er] a gleba amoveri non poterunt, quamdiu solvere possunt debitas pensiones; I 11, 1f. 7 (bessere so o. II 300 n. 10b)

Ibid. Bauer 10b; Fron. According to Dial. de scacc. I 10 C. 11 B.C, it is true that at first after 1066 the Anglo-Saxons [on village land, in peasant holdings] might pro voluntate dominorum a possessionibus pell[i], but they then obtained secure possession, and only the demesne ascriptitii a dominis suis ad alia loca transferri possunt, venduntur vel distrahuntur. That supervision by the state of the relationship between manor and villein, directed against the eviction or transplanting of villeins occasionally attested in the 12th cent., is older than the period of Henry II, in which the royal courts lost jurisdiction over villeins; Vinogradoff Villain. 159. 165. 219; Maitland Domesday 62.—Perhaps Bracton had this sentence of L before him: former free peasants on ‘ancient demesne of the Crown’ [he speaks only of that] a gleba amoveri non poterunt, quamdiu solvere possunt debitas pensiones; I 11, 1f. 7 (correct accordingly above II 300 n. 10b)
